summary: Describes extensions to LSP ping so it can verify connectivity and trace routes for MPLS Transport Profile LSPs and pseudowires on demand. It also clarifies how related operations messages should be handled. It updates RFC 4379.

plainLanguage.summary: LSP ping checks an MPLS path on demand by sending a test packet along it and waiting for the answer. It assumes the routers have IP addresses and that the path was set up by a signalling protocol. MPLS Transport Profile paths often have neither, so the test could not be run on them. This RFC extends the mechanism so it works without IP addresses, so a statically configured path or a pseudowire can be named and tested, and so that the return path can be checked as well.

subtitle: How to extend LSP ping so operators can test and trace MPLS Transport Profile paths, even without IP addresses.

tldr.problem: LSP ping, the standard way to check an MPLS path on demand, assumes the routers have IP addresses and that the path was set up by a signalling protocol. MPLS Transport Profile paths are often managed without IP addressing, and a statically configured path or a pseudowire cannot be named in the request at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends LSP ping with a downstream mapping address type for use without IP, a new associated channel type, identifier TLVs that name the source and destination nodes, and target FEC sub-TLVs that name statically provisioned LSPs and pseudowires. It also adds a flag that asks the far end to prove the return path.
tldr.outcome: Connectivity verification and route tracing now work on MPLS-TP paths with or without IP addressing, and a bidirectional path can be checked in both directions from a single request.

today: RFC 6426 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes it. It updates RFC 4379 by adding an address type and creating a registry for downstream mapping address types, and it is the Standards Track extension that carries LSP ping into MPLS Transport Profile networks.

sections.title: What LSP Ping Does and What MPLS-TP Needs
sections.content:
Label Switched Path ping (LSP ping), defined in RFC 4379, is an Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanism for MPLS label switched paths (LSPs). This RFC describes extensions to it so that LSP ping can be used for on-demand monitoring of MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) LSPs and pseudowires, and it clarifies the procedures for processing the related OAM packets. It meets the on-demand connectivity verification and route tracing requirements of RFC 5860, as specified in RFC 6371, and it updates RFC 4379 by adding a new address type and creating an IANA registry.

The RFC is careful about its own vocabulary, because three terms are easily confused. LSP ping is the mechanism. On-demand CV means on-demand connectivity verification and, where both apply equally, on-demand route tracing, implemented with the LSP ping mechanism extended for MPLS-TP. On-demand route tracing is used where the extended mechanism is used exclusively for route tracing. Two roles appear throughout: the Requester originates an OAM request message, and the Responder answers it. All messages are carried in an LSP, so a request is injected at the ingress of an LSP, and a responder may or may not sit at the egress of that same LSP, because it can also receive requests when the time-to-live (TTL) expires along the way.

The gap the extensions close is that LSP ping normally requires IP addressing on the responding routers. The echo packets are encapsulated in an IP/UDP header with a destination address from the 127/8 range and then in the MPLS label stack, and a responder recognises OAM packets by that destination address and the UDP port number. This does not need IP forwarding, but it does need an IP host stack on the router. In MPLS-TP deployments where IP addressing is not available, or where a non-IP encapsulation is preferred, on-demand CV and route tracing SHOULD be run without IP addressing, using the associated channel (ACH) mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage:
LSP ping checks an MPLS path on demand by sending a test packet along it and waiting for the answer. It assumes the routers have IP addresses and that the path was set up by a signalling protocol. MPLS Transport Profile paths often have neither, so the test could not be run on them at all.

This RFC makes the test work without IP addresses, and makes it possible to name a path that was configured by hand rather than by a protocol, and to check that the return path is the right one.

sections.title: New Fields in the LSP Ping Message
sections.content:
The RFC adds four groups of fields to the LSP ping message.

The Downstream Mapping (DSMAP) TLV of RFC 4379, and the Downstream Detailed Mapping (DDMAP) TLV of RFC 6424, gain a new address type, number 5, named Non IP, with 12 octets. It means that no address is present in the TLV, but the ingress and egress interface numbers (IF_Num) and the multipath information may still be there. An IF_Num of zero means that no interface number applies in that field, and the multipath type SHOULD be set to zero. When this address type is used, interface verification MUST be bypassed on receipt of an echo request, so the receiving node SHOULD only perform MPLS label control plane and data plane consistency checks, which include checking the included identifier information.

A Source Identifier TLV and a Destination Identifier TLV are defined, of type 13 and 14, each eight octets long and each holding a four-octet Global ID and a four-octet Node ID as defined in RFC 6370. The Source Identifier TLV names the originator of the packet and the Destination Identifier TLV names the destination node. An on-demand CV packet MUST NOT carry more than one of either; if it does, and the source can still be identified unambiguously, the error for a malformed echo request MUST be returned.

To name a statically provisioned LSP or pseudowire in an echo request, two new Target FEC Stack sub-TLVs are defined: sub-type 22 for a static LSP, 24 octets long, and sub-type 23 for a static pseudowire, 32 octets long. The static LSP sub-TLV carries the source and destination Global ID and Node ID, the source tunnel number, the LSP number and a destination tunnel number that must be zero. The static pseudowire sub-TLV carries a 64-bit service identifier, the source and destination Global ID and Node ID, and the source and destination AC-ID fields defined in RFC 5003. Either Global ID may be set to zero, which means the field does not apply, for example where local scope is enough to identify the service.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds four things to the test packet. A new address type for the field that records where the packet went, meaning there is no IP address to record, only interface numbers. Two small identifier fields, one naming the node that sent the packet and one naming the node it was sent to, so a receiver can tell whether the packet came from where it expected. Two new ways of naming the path under test, one for a path configured by hand and one for a pseudowire. And a way of saying that a statically configured path may be identified by local names alone, by leaving the global identifier zero.

sections.title: Running the Check
sections.content:
The on-demand CV function meets the requirements of Section 2.2.3 of RFC 5860. It SHOULD NOT be performed except in the on-demand mode, and it SHOULD be performed between the end points and intermediate points of PWs and LSPs, and between the end points of PWs, LSPs and sections. For the packet to be processed at the intermediate point being probed, the TTL of the MPLS label MUST be set so that it expires there.

With IP encapsulation, the echo request travels along the LSP under test with an IP/UDP packet inside it. The IP header is not used for forwarding, since MPLS does the forwarding, but it is used for addressing. This form of on-demand CV MUST be supported for MPLS-TP LSPs when IP addressing is in use. The response MUST be sent on the reverse path of the LSP, with IP/UDP headers followed by the payload, the destination address set to that of the sender of the request and the source address set to a valid address of the replying node.

IP encapsulated packets MAY also be sent over the LSP's control channel, using the IP associated channel type of RFC 4385. A new pseudowire associated channel type, 0x0025, is defined for on-demand connectivity verification, and ACH TLVs SHALL NOT be associated with it.

Without IP encapsulation, the on-demand CV request payload MUST directly follow the ACH header, and the reply mode in the echo request SHOULD be set to 4, reply via application level control channel. The reply MUST then be sent on the reverse path of the LSP using ACH, with the payload directly following the ACH header and with no IP or UDP headers attached. A node that receives such a request but has no return MPLS LSP path to the source SHOULD drop it. A node that receives a request with a reply mode other than 4 MAY answer using that mode if it supports it, and MUST drop the request if it does not support the requested mode.
sections.plainLanguage:
There are three ways to run the check. With IP addresses, the test packet is carried inside the path with an IP and UDP header, and the answer comes back along the reverse path. With IP addresses but over the path's control channel, the same thing happens with the packet wrapped differently. Without IP addresses at all, the payload follows the control channel header directly, and the request asks for the answer to come back that way too.

In every case the answer comes back along a path, and a node that has no way to send the answer back drops the request rather than guessing.

sections.title: Checking the Return Path Too
sections.content:
A new global flag, Validate Reverse Path (R), is defined in the LSP ping packet header. When it is set in an echo request, the responder SHOULD return reverse-path FEC information. The R flag MUST NOT be set in an echo response. The global flags field is now a bit vector holding the R flag alongside the V flag defined in RFC 4379 and the T flag defined in RFC 6425. The Validate FEC Stack (V) flag MAY be set in the echo response when reverse-path connectivity verification is being performed.

When the R flag is set, the responding node SHOULD attach a Reverse-path Target FEC Stack TLV to the echo response. Its format is the same as that of the Target FEC Stack TLV of RFC 4379, and the rules for creating a Target FEC Stack TLV also apply to it. Its type is 16. For a co-routed bidirectional LSP the reverse-path Target FEC Stack is the same in both directions; for an associated bidirectional LSP it MAY be different for the reverse path.

On receipt of the echo response, the requesting node MUST perform interface and label stack validation to confirm that the packet was received on the reverse path of the bidirectional LSP, and MUST perform FEC validation if the Reverse-path Target FEC Stack TLV is present, using the procedure of Section 3.6 of RFC 4379. If any of those validations fail, the requesting node MUST drop the echo response and SHOULD log and/or report an error.
sections.plainLanguage: One extra check is available: the requester can ask the far end to prove which path the answer came back on. The far end adds a field describing the reverse path, and the requester then checks that the packet arrived on the right interface with the right labels and that the path description matches. If any of that fails, the answer is thrown away and the error is recorded.

sections.title: Tracing the Route
sections.content:
On-demand route tracing meets the route tracing requirement of Section 2.2.3 of RFC 5860. It SHOULD be performed on demand, between the end points and intermediate points of PWs and LSPs, and between the end points of PWs, LSPs and sections.

The requesting node inserts a Downstream Mapping TLV to get information about the downstream node and to enable LSP verification along the transit nodes. The TLV can be used as it is defined for route tracing, and where IP addressing is not in use the address type field can be set to Non IP. With IP encapsulation the mechanics are the same as for the check described earlier, and this form MUST be supported for MPLS-TP LSPs when IP addressing is in use. Without IP encapsulation, the request packets take the same form as in the non-IP case above, and MPLS TTL expiry is used to direct the packets to specific nodes along the path. The responses are received on the LSP itself, and the presence of an ACH header with the on-demand CV channel type indicates that the packet carries an on-demand CV payload. At the responder, the CV data, the label stack and the destination identifier together are enough to identify the LSP. If there is an error and the node cannot identify the LSP on which the response would be sent, it MUST drop the request and send nothing back. All responses MUST be sent on an LSP path using the ACH header and the on-demand CV channel type.

Point-to-multipoint LSPs are covered as well: the procedures of RFC 6425 MUST be supported for MPLS-TP P2MP LSPs when IP addressing is used, and the non-IP procedures can be applied to them as well. One limitation is stated: on-demand CV using ACH SHOULD NOT be used when there is Equal Cost Multi-Path for a given LSP, because the additional ACH header can modify the hashing behaviour for OAM packets and so give a wrong picture of the path taken by the data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage:
Route tracing finds out which nodes the path actually goes through. The requester sends the test packet with a time-to-live set so that it expires at one hop, reads the answer, then repeats with a longer life to reach the next hop. The answer describes the node that answered, which is what lets the requester build the route.

There is one warning. If the network spreads traffic over several equal-cost paths, the extra header this method adds can change how packets are hashed, and the test would then follow a different path from the real traffic.

sections.title: When These Procedures Apply
sections.content:
The procedures for non-IP encapsulation apply to MPLS-TP transport paths, which includes LSPs and PWs when IP encapsulation is not wanted. Where IP addressing is used, as in ordinary non MPLS-TP LSPs, the procedures of RFC 4379 MUST be used.

Two operational points appear elsewhere in the document. Support for on-demand CV on a static MPLS-TP LSP or pseudowire MAY require manageable objects, for instance to configure operating parameters such as the identifiers associated with a statically configured LSP or PW; the specifics of that requirement are out of scope and SHOULD be addressed in management specifications. And at the requester, when the echo request is encapsulated with the IP or the non-IP ACH codepoint, a Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) MUST be added before the MPLS LSP label. The GAL MUST NOT be treated as part of the MPLS label stack that the responder verifies, so no Nil FEC TLV may be added or associated with it, and the GAL MUST NOT be included in DSMAP or DDMAP TLVs. Interface and Label Stack TLVs, on the other hand, MUST include the whole label stack including the GAL.
sections.plainLanguage:
These procedures are for transport paths that do not use IP addresses. Ordinary MPLS paths that do use IP keep using the original procedure.

Two practical details are worth knowing. A statically configured path may need extra configuration objects so that its identifiers can be set. And the test packet carries one extra label, the generic associated channel label, in front of the path's own labels. That extra label is not part of what the far end checks, but it does have to appear in the interface and label stack fields.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no new security considerations of its own, and those discussed in RFC 4379 apply to it. It notes one difference from the typical deployments that document assumes: on-demand CV for transport paths is likely to be used across MPLS administrative boundaries. Where that may occur, it is RECOMMENDED that on-demand OAM is configured as necessary to ensure that Source Identifier TLVs are included in on-demand CV messages, which allows implementations to filter OAM messages arriving from an unexpected or unknown source.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security rules. It does point out that these checks are likely to run between networks with different owners, and recommends that every message then carries the identifier of the node that sent it, so that a receiver can drop messages from a source it does not expect.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has assigned two TLV types from the MPLS LSPs Ping Parameters registry: 13 for the Source ID TLV and 14 for the Destination ID TLV, each eight octets long. Two sub-TLV types have been assigned for inclusion in the Target FEC Stack TLV, 22 for Static LSP and 23 for Static Pseudowire. A new TLV type, 16, has been assigned for the Reverse-path Target FEC Stack TLV; its sub-TLV space and assignments are the same as those of the Target FEC Stack TLV, and any new sub-type added to the Target FEC Stack TLV MUST apply to it as well.

A PW ACH Type of 0x0025 has been allocated for on-demand CV, with no TLV following it. Finally, a new Downstream Mapping Address Type registry has been established, covering both RFC 4379 and this document: type 1 IPv4 Numbered, 2 IPv4 Unnumbered, 3 IPv6 Numbered, 4 IPv6 Unnumbered and 5 Non IP. The field is 8 bits wide, so the allocation policy for the registry is Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks for seven new numbers to be reserved: two for the source and destination identifiers, two for naming a static path or pseudowire, one for the reverse path description, one for the new channel type, and one for the address type registry.
